source.text: The growth file is refreshed on demand, not by the commit hook. Every commit shifts the last frame, so a hook that regenerated the file would make every commit touch it. The session counts are rebuilt daily by the laptop daemon, as above. Each file's `generated` field is also the day the script ran, so the same inputs give different bytes on different days. Nothing flags a stale growth file: compare `generated` with today. To refresh the web-tools growth file, run the first command from the root of an unshallowed clone, with `.` as the clone, `data/doc-growth/web-tools.json` as the output, and `--name mehrlander/web-tools`. The chart's last sample counts every recorded session, so session counts newer than the growth file still show in full there.

checks.answer: No. Every commit shifts the last frame, so a hook that regenerated the growth file would make every commit touch it. The file is refreshed on demand instead, not by the commit hook.
Compare the file's `generated` field (the day the script ran) with today's date. Nothing warns or flags a stale growth file; the reader has to make that comparison themselves.

Run the first command (the growth script; the paragraph does not name it) from the root of an unshallowed clone, passing `.` as the clone, `data/doc-growth/web-tools.json` as the output, and `--name mehrlander/web-tools`.
Not a fault. Each file's `generated` field is the day the script ran, so the same inputs give different bytes on different days.

The laptop daemon rebuilds the session counts daily. Yes, the newer counts still show in full on the chart before the growth file is refreshed, because the chart's last sample counts every recorded session.
